course.title: Queues & backlog math
course.description: Queue and backlog reps for the async part of a system-design interview: when one job in the queue will actually run (per-job ETAs), turning a freshness SLA into the backlog threshold you alert on, how many consumers it takes to drain a lag before a deadline while arrivals continue, how retries at every layer multiply into an exponential storm, sizing a dead-letter queue, batching requests against someone else's rate limit, the backlog a fan-out-on-write timeline creates, and how much load you must shed during overload. Every drill is whole-number arithmetic with the conversions named (86,400 s/day; per-mille = parts per thousand = x/1000), so you practise the reasoning, not the calculator.

sysdrills/09-queues-and-backlog/01-queue.instructions:
**Skills:** queues · latency  
**Level:** ★☆☆

**Interview prompt.** "Your export queue shows 1,200 jobs ahead of mine; 4 workers each take 2 s per job. When does my export finish?"

**Why it works.** With `workers` identical workers each finishing a job every `jobSec` seconds, the head of the queue advances `workers` jobs per `jobSec` — the pool's throughput, not one worker's. A job with k jobs ahead waits `k × jobSec ÷ workers` seconds for its turn, then runs for its own `jobSec`. This is the user-facing number ("position 1,200 — about 10 minutes"), not the time to empty the whole queue. The tests choose inputs that divide exactly, so every answer is a whole number.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `queueWaitSec(jobsAhead, workers, jobSec)` → `jobsAhead × jobSec ÷ workers`
- `jobEtaSec(jobsAhead, workers, jobSec)` → `queueWaitSec(…) + jobSec`

**Worked example.** 1,200 ahead, 4 workers, 2 s/job → wait 1,200 × 2 ÷ 4 = 600 s → done at **602 s** (~10 minutes).
sysdrills/09-queues-and-backlog/01-queue.explanation:
The pool, not one worker, advances the queue.

For `jobEtaSec(1200, 4, 2)`:
- the 4 workers finish 4 jobs every 2 s, so 1,200 jobs ahead take 1,200 × 2 ÷ 4 = 600 s
- add the job's own 2 s run → **602 s**

This is the number to show users ("~10 minutes") instead of a spinner — queue position ÷ pool throughput, a different question from how long the WHOLE backlog takes to drain (module 06).
hints: The whole pool advances the queue: 4 workers at 2 s each finish 2 jobs every second, not one job every 2 s.
wait = jobsAhead × jobSec ÷ workers; eta = wait + jobSec.
The queue advances workers jobs every jobSec, so the wait is jobsAhead × jobSec ÷ workers — add your own jobSec on top for the finish time

sysdrills/09-queues-and-backlog/02-backl.instructions:
**Skills:** queues · slo  
**Level:** ★★☆

**Interview prompt.** "Product says every job must start within 5 minutes of being enqueued. The workers process 200 jobs/s. What backlog should page someone — and right now there are 90,000 jobs queued: how many will start late?"

**Why it works.** A job at the back of a queue of size B starts after B ÷ processPerSec seconds. Requiring that to be at most `slaSec` means B ≤ processPerSec × slaSec — the freshness SLA turns into ONE backlog number you can alert on (5 minutes = 300 s). Every job beyond that threshold is already doomed to start late even if nothing else arrives, so the late count is the excess over the threshold, never below zero.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `maxHealthyBacklog(processPerSec, slaSec)` → `processPerSec × slaSec`
- `jobsOverSla(backlog, processPerSec, slaSec)` → `max(0, backlog − processPerSec × slaSec)`

**Worked example.** 200 jobs/s with a 300 s SLA → threshold 200 × 300 = **60,000** jobs; alert when the backlog crosses it.
sysdrills/09-queues-and-backlog/02-backl.explanation:
The SLA times the processing rate is the backlog you can afford; everything above it is already late.

For `jobsOverSla(90000, 200, 300)`:
- threshold = 200 × 300 = 60,000 jobs
- 90,000 − 60,000 = **30,000** jobs will start late no matter what

Page on backlog > rate × SLA, not on a vibes number like "10k messages" — the threshold moves whenever the processing rate or the SLA does.
hints: The last job in a queue of size B waits B ÷ processPerSec seconds before it starts — set that wait equal to the SLA.
threshold = processPerSec × slaSec; late = max(0, backlog − threshold).
The largest healthy backlog is processPerSec × slaSec — anything above that is already doomed, so subtract the threshold from the backlog and clamp at zero

sysdrills/09-queues-and-backlog/03-consu.instructions:
**Skills:** queues · capacity  
**Level:** ★★☆

**Interview prompt.** "Kafka consumer lag is 600,000 messages, producers keep writing 2,000 messages/s, and each consumer handles 500 messages/s. We must be caught up within 10 minutes. How many consumers do we run?"

**Why it works.** Work conservation: over the `drainSec` window the fleet must process the existing backlog PLUS everything that arrives during the window (arrivePerSec × drainSec). One consumer does perConsumerPerSec × drainSec in the window, so the fleet size is total work ÷ one consumer's work, rounded UP to whole consumers (10 minutes = 600 s). Once caught up, the fleet's surplus (fleet rate − arrival rate) tells you whether the backlog shrinks (positive) or still grows (negative).

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `consumersToDrain(backlog, drainSec, arrivePerSec, perConsumerPerSec)` → `ceil((backlog + arrivePerSec × drainSec) ÷ (drainSec × perConsumerPerSec))`
- `surplusPerSec(consumers, perConsumerPerSec, arrivePerSec)` → `consumers × perConsumerPerSec − arrivePerSec` (negative = the backlog still grows)

**Worked example.** 600,000 lag, 600 s, 2,000/s arriving, 500/s per consumer → work = 600,000 + 2,000 × 600 = 1,800,000; one consumer does 500 × 600 = 300,000 → **6** consumers exactly.
sysdrills/09-queues-and-backlog/03-consu.explanation:
Arrivals keep landing WHILE you drain, so they belong in the work total.

For `consumersToDrain(600000, 600, 2000, 400)`:
- work in the window = 600,000 + 2,000 × 600 = 1,800,000 messages
- one consumer does 400 × 600 = 240,000 in the window
- 1,800,000 ÷ 240,000 = 7.5 → rounds UP to **8**

And remember 07/08: partitions cap how many consumers in a group can actually run, so check the partition count before promising 8.
hints: Over the window the fleet must clear the backlog AND everything that arrives during the window.
consumers = ⌈(backlog + arrive × drainSec) ÷ (drainSec × perConsumer)⌉; surplus = consumers × perConsumer − arrive.

Total work in the window is the backlog plus arrivals during it (arrive × seconds) — divide by one consumer's work in the window (rate × seconds) and round up, and the surplus is fleet rate minus arrival rate

sysdrills/09-queues-and-backlog/04-retry.instructions:
**Skills:** retries · architecture  
**Level:** ★★★

**Interview prompt.** "A request goes client → API → service → database, and every layer retries failed calls up to 3 attempts. The database dies. How much load actually hits it?"

**Why it works.** Retries MULTIPLY per layer. If the database is down, the service makes 3 attempts per call it receives; the API makes 3 attempts at the service, each of which becomes 3 database attempts; the client does the same to the API. With `depth` retrying layers each allowing `attemptsPerCall` attempts, one user request becomes attemptsPerCall^depth attempts at the bottom — linear retry math gone exponential. Zero retrying layers means just the request itself (factor 1).

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `attemptsPerUserRequest(attemptsPerCall, depth)` → `attemptsPerCall` multiplied together `depth` times, starting from 1 (use a loop)
- `bottomLayerQps(baseQps, attemptsPerCall, depth)` → `baseQps × attemptsPerUserRequest(attemptsPerCall, depth)`

**Worked example.** 3 attempts per call through 3 retrying layers → 3 × 3 × 3 = **27** attempts per user request.
sysdrills/09-queues-and-backlog/04-retry.explanation:
Each layer multiplies what the layer above sends it.

For `bottomLayerQps(1000, 3, 3)`:
- amplification = 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 attempts per user request
- 1,000 × 27 = **27,000** QPS pounding the dead database at the worst moment

Retry at ONE layer only (usually the edge) — this is 06/07's linear base × attempts gone exponential through a call chain, and 04/06's cascade argument in load form.
hints: If the database is down, every layer above it sees every call fail and retries each one — those retries stack.
factor = attemptsPerCall^depth; bottom QPS = baseQps × factor.
Each retrying layer multiplies attempts by attemptsPerCall, so multiply 1 by attemptsPerCall once per layer of depth — the bottom-layer load is base QPS × that factor

sysdrills/09-queues-and-backlog/05-dlq-s.instructions:
**Skills:** queues · storage  
**Level:** ★☆☆

**Interview prompt.** "We process 8,640,000 messages a day (100/s). About 5‰ fail every retry and land in the dead-letter queue, messages are 2,000 bytes, and we keep dead letters 14 days for replay. How big does the DLQ get?"

**Why it works.** The DLQ inflow is the failing per-mille slice of the day's traffic: messagesPerDay × failPermille ÷ 1000 (per-mille = ‰ = x/1000; 86,400 s/day × 100/s = 8,640,000/day). Nothing leaves the DLQ until someone replays or the retention window expires, so its steady-state size is a day's dead letters × bytes per message × retention days. The tests choose inputs that divide exactly, so every answer is a whole number.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `dlqPerDay(messagesPerDay, failPermille)` → `messagesPerDay × failPermille ÷ 1000`
- `dlqBytes(messagesPerDay, failPermille, bytesPerMessage, retentionDays)` → `dlqPerDay(…) × bytesPerMessage × retentionDays`

**Worked example.** 8,640,000 messages/day at 5‰ → 8,640,000 × 5 ÷ 1000 = **43,200** dead letters a day.
sysdrills/09-queues-and-backlog/05-dlq-s.explanation:
The failure per-mille sets the inflow; retention sets how long it piles up.

For `dlqBytes(8640000, 5, 2000, 14)`:
- dead letters per day = 8,640,000 × 5 ÷ 1000 = 43,200
- 43,200 × 2,000 B = 86,400,000 bytes per day
- × 14 days = **1,209,600,000** bytes (~1.2 GB)

A DLQ is a buffer you size and alert on, not a dumpster — and the outage case (1000‰ for a day), not the happy case, sets the size.
hints: Only the failing slice of traffic reaches the DLQ, and it stays there for the whole retention window.
perDay = messages × fail‰ ÷ 1000; bytes = perDay × bytesPerMessage × retentionDays.
The dead-letter inflow is the failing per-mille slice of the day's messages (messages × fail‰ ÷ 1000) — multiply by bytes per message and the retention days for the storage

sysdrills/09-queues-and-backlog/06-batch.instructions:
**Skills:** batching · rate-limiting  
**Level:** ★★☆

**Interview prompt.** "The nightly sync pushes 1,000,000 records to a partner API capped at 50 requests/s. The API accepts batches of up to 500 records. How long does the sync take batched versus one record per request?"

**Why it works.** The rate limit counts REQUESTS, not records, so batching is the only lever you control. The request count is items ÷ batchSize rounded UP — a partial last batch still costs one whole request. Duration is then the request count ÷ the allowed requests per second. The tests choose inputs that divide exactly, so every duration is a whole number.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `requestsNeeded(items, batchSize)` → `ceil(items ÷ batchSize)`
- `sendSeconds(items, batchSize, requestsPerSec)` → `requestsNeeded(items, batchSize) ÷ requestsPerSec`

**Worked example.** 1,000,000 records in batches of 500 → ceil(1,000,000 ÷ 500) = **2,000** requests.
sysdrills/09-queues-and-backlog/06-batch.explanation:
The limiter sees requests, so fewer, fuller requests finish sooner.

For `sendSeconds(1000000, 500, 50)`:
- requests = ceil(1,000,000 ÷ 500) = 2,000
- 2,000 ÷ 50/s = **40 s**
- versus 1,000,000 ÷ 50 = 20,000 s (~5½ h) sent one by one

Under someone else's rate limit, batch size is the only lever you have — ask for the maximum batch size before you ask for a higher limit.
hints: The rate limit only counts requests — how many records ride in each request is up to you.
requests = ⌈items ÷ batchSize⌉; seconds = requests ÷ requestsPerSec.
Requests are items ÷ batchSize rounded up because a partial batch still costs one request — divide the request count by the allowed requests per second for the duration

sysdrills/09-queues-and-backlog/07-fanou.instructions:
**Skills:** queues · fan-out  
**Level:** ★★☆

**Interview prompt.** "Our timeline is push-based: every post becomes one delivery job per follower. Users post 100 times a second with 200 followers on average. Then a celebrity with 50,000,000 followers posts and the delivery workers top out at 100,000 writes/s. What happens?"

**Why it works.** Fan-out on write turns every post into `followers` timeline writes, so steady-state delivery load is postsPerSec × avgFollowers. One celebrity post enqueues `followers` writes at once; at a capped delivery rate the LAST follower sees the post only after followers ÷ cap seconds. The tests choose inputs that divide exactly, so every answer is a whole number.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `deliveriesPerSec(postsPerSec, avgFollowers)` → `postsPerSec × avgFollowers`
- `celebrityLagSec(followers, deliveriesPerSecCap)` → `followers ÷ deliveriesPerSecCap`

**Worked example.** 100 posts/s × 200 followers → **20,000** timeline writes per second.
sysdrills/09-queues-and-backlog/07-fanou.explanation:
Fan-out multiplies one write by the follower count.

For `celebrityLagSec(50000000, 100000)`:
- one post = 50,000,000 timeline writes
- 50,000,000 ÷ 100,000 deliveries/s = **500 s** (~8 minutes) before the LAST follower's timeline has the post

This one number is why real feeds go hybrid — push for normal users, pull (merge at read time) for celebrities.
hints: Push-model timelines copy each post into every follower's timeline, so a post costs one write per follower.
deliveries/s = postsPerSec × avgFollowers; lag = followers ÷ cap.
Every post becomes one timeline write per follower, so deliveries per second is posts × average followers — one celebrity post queues followers ÷ the delivery rate seconds of work

sysdrills/09-queues-and-backlog/08-load-.instructions:
**Skills:** overload · throughput  
**Level:** ★☆☆

**Interview prompt.** "The service can handle 20,000 requests/s. A traffic spike brings 50,000/s. How much must we reject to keep the requests we admit fast?"

**Why it works.** A server pushed past capacity does not serve capacity-worth of requests slowly — queues grow without bound and EVERY request times out. Shedding the excess at the door (fast 503s) keeps the admitted requests within latency. The excess is arrivals − capacity, never below zero; as a share of traffic it is shed × 1000 ÷ arrivals in per-mille (‰ = x/1000). `shedPermille` is only called with arrivals above zero, and the tests choose inputs that divide exactly, so every answer is a whole number.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `shedPerSec(arrivePerSec, capacityPerSec)` → `max(0, arrivePerSec − capacityPerSec)`
- `shedPermille(arrivePerSec, capacityPerSec)` → `shedPerSec(…) × 1000 ÷ arrivePerSec`

**Worked example.** 30,000/s arriving at a 20,000/s service → shed **10,000/s**.

Reject the excess so the rest stays fast.

For `shedPermille(50000, 20000)`:
- shed = 50,000 − 20,000 = 30,000/s
- 30,000 × 1000 ÷ 50,000 = **600‰**

At 2.5× overload you reject 60% so the 40% you admit stay fast; admit everything and 100% of users get timeouts.
hints: Past capacity, admitting more does not serve more — it makes every request slow. Only the excess has to go.
shed = max(0, arrive − capacity); shed‰ = shed × 1000 ÷ arrive.
Whatever arrives above capacity must be rejected: the shed rate is arrivals minus capacity clamped at zero — scale by 1000 ÷ arrivals for the per-mille share
